title: Why Is My Cat Spraying? Causes, Myths & How to Stop It
summary: Why is your cat spraying? Discover common causes, myths, and vet-backed tips to stop spraying, reduce stress, and prevent it from happening again.

If you've ever dealt with a cat that sprays, you'll know how frustrating it can be. In fact, tragically, it’s one of the more common reasons cats are abandoned at shelters. So, many people feel like their cat is acting out or being spiteful. But the fact is, that's almost never the case. Spraying is a natural behavior, and once you understand why your cat is doing it, it's much easier to address.


**Content:**


1. What Is Cat Spraying? Signs, Causes & How to Tell It Apart From Peeing
2. Male vs. Female Cat Spraying: Does Neutering or Spaying Stop It?
3. How to Stop a Cat From Spraying: Training & Behavior Strategies
4. Is Spraying a Cat With Water OK? Common Myths About Punishment
5. Conclusion


## What Is Cat Spraying? Signs, Causes & How to Tell It Apart From Peeing


Spraying isn't the same as normal urination. While cats usually squat to empty their bladder into the litter box (hopefully), spraying involves backing up to a vertical surface with a raised tail and releasing a small amount of pee.


As veterinary behaviorist[Dr. Debra Horwitz](http://www.animalbehavior.net/Bio/DebraHorwitzbio.htm?ref=petcube.com) explains:


> "Urine spraying is a form of communication that utilizes olfactory and visual cues to transmit information."


In other words, your cat isn't trying to annoy you; they're leaving a message that’s part of normal feline behavior. They do it to mark territory, communicate with other cats or respond to stress and changes in their environment.


## Male vs. Female Cat Spraying: Does Neutering or Spaying Stop It?


Male cats are more likely to spray than females, especially if they haven't been neutered. Neutering usually reduces spraying in many cats because it lowers hormone levels that drive territorial marking. But not always.


One[redditor](https://www.reddit.com/r/CatTraining/comments/1haiao0/cat_spraying_ruining_everything/?ref=petcube.com) vents their frustration when they wrote:


> "my male kitty pickles is a bit over 2 years old and is neutered. ever since we neutered him a little over a year ago, he’s been spraying everywhere. the walls, curtains, kitchen, counters, sinks floors, literally anything he sees he will pee on."


However, as the Reddit post above shows, it's not a guaranteed cure. Some neutered males (and even some female cats) keep spraying if the behavior has become a habit or if they're feeling stressed and anxious; or threatened by changes in their environment.


## How to Stop a Cat From Spraying: Training & Behavior Strategies


The first step is ruling out medical problems. If your cat suddenly starts spraying, schedule a veterinary visit to make sure there isn't a[urinary tract issue](https://petcube.com/blog/uti-medicine-for-cats/) or another health concern.


If you are sure your cat is healthy, look for possible stressors. Felines are extremely sensitive. Some of the things that can trigger spraying include:


- new pet,
- moving house,
- unfamilar visitors,
- neighborhood cats outside the window,
- or changes to your daily routine.


To deal with these issues, focus on reducing stress, keeping a predictable routine, and giving them safe spaces where they feel secure.


If you're unsure what's triggering the behavior, the[Petcube App](https://petcube.com/mobile-app/?ref=petcube.com) can help you track behavior to find triggers and give you access to 24/7 AI health guidance to help find the best strategy for your cat.


## Is Spraying a Cat With Water OK? Common Myths About Punishment


No. Spraying your cat with water or using other forms of punishment won't teach them why spraying is unwanted. Instead, it often increases[fear and stress](https://petcube.com/blog/how-to-comfort-a-scared-cat/) , which can actually make the behavior worse. Most animals don’t respond well to punishment, but cats specifically respond badly to it.


Remember, to a cat, spraying is just communication. If you punish the behavior without addressing the underlying cause, they may simply become more[anxious](https://petcube.com/blog/cat-separation-anxiety/) while continuing to spray.


## Conclusion


Cat spraying can be messy and frustrating, but it isn't your cat trying to get revenge or misbehave. In most cases, it's your cat's way of communicating that something isn't right. The trick is to identify the cause and remove it, or otherwise reduce stress. Be patient and never resort to punishment.
